title: Identifying the appliance and reading the manufacturer's care instructions
referencesAtStart: Official references for this lesson: ACCC, Consumer rights and guarantees (business page) (no date in body; page metadata shows 17 July 2026).
moduleTitle: Shared: Job management and service delivery
audience: Workers who clean specialty appliances and need to confirm what they are cleaning and how the manufacturer allows it to be cleaned
learningOutcomes: Identify an appliance's make, model and serial number from its data plate and label
Find and read the manufacturer's care and cleaning instructions for the model
Record the pre-clean condition of an appliance, including damage, leaks and fault codes
Decide whether a cleaning method is allowed for a specific appliance and finish

instruction.heading: Know what you are cleaning before you touch it
instruction.body: Two machines that look alike can have different care rules. A commercial dishwasher from one manufacturer may allow a rinse of the spray arms, while a model from another manufacturer may forbid water on the same part. Before you clean, locate the data plate. It is usually on the back, side or inside the door frame and carries the make, model and serial number. Copy these into the job record. If the plate is missing or unreadable, record that fact and the visible brand and model, and treat the appliance as having unknown care rules. Unknown rules mean you use the most conservative method you have been trained in, which is dry removal of debris and a light damp wipe with an approved product, and you stay away from any part that carries a warning label.

instruction.heading: Read the manufacturer's care instructions first
instruction.body: The manufacturer's care and cleaning instructions are the first reference for every method. They are often in the owner's manual, in the installation guide, or on the manufacturer's website. Your business should hold the link to the correct manual for each machine in the equipment record, and it should be checked before the job. When you read the instructions, look for four things: which parts may be cleaned by the user, which cleaning products are approved, which methods are forbidden, such as direct spray or steam on certain parts, and any warranty statements about cleaning or third-party work. Where the manual and the business procedure disagree, the more protective instruction governs, and you report the disagreement to the supervisor. Do not rely on a memory of how a model used to be cleaned, because manufacturers change their guidance between model years.

instruction.heading: Record the condition before you start
instruction.body: A pre-clean record protects you, the customer and the business. Walk around the appliance and note anything that is already wrong. Look for leaks or wet patches on the floor under the machine, cracked or missing panels, loose or hanging covers, scorch marks, a burnt smell, unusual sounds when it is idle, damaged door seals, and any fault code on the display. Photograph each point with the appliance and its data plate in the frame. Do not test the machine by running it. If the machine is running when you arrive, record that it is running and go to the isolation step in lesson “Making a machine safe before cleaning: isolation, stored energy and moving parts” before you do anything else. A fault that you find before the job is a fault you did not cause, and the record should say so clearly. If you find a fault that is outside the course, stop, record it and refer it, as in lesson “Scope, authority and exclusions for appliance cleaning”.

procedure: Check the booking for the appliance make, model and location, and open the equipment record for the linked manufacturer manual.
Find the data plate and record the make, model and serial number. If it cannot be read, record the visible brand and model and note that the plate is missing.
Read the manufacturer's care and cleaning section for the model, and note the parts you may clean, the approved products and the forbidden methods.
Walk around the appliance and record any existing damage, leaks, loose panels, scorch marks, odours or fault codes, with a photograph of each.
If the appliance is running, stop, do not start any cleaning, and go to the isolation procedure before you go further.
Decide the cleaning method for each part, marking any part where the rules are unknown as out of scope until the supervisor confirms.
Confirm the record with the site contact and note any condition they report that you did not see.

workedExamples.situation: You arrive to clean the exterior of a commercial dishwasher. The data plate on the rear is painted over. The fascia is greasy and the floor under the machine has a shallow wet patch. The display shows a fault code.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you start cleaning the fascia, and what do you record?
workedExamples.reasoning: The model is not known, the care rules are not known, and there is a leak and a fault code. Do not start cleaning yet. Record the painted plate, the brand and visible model, the wet patch with a photograph, and the fault code. Do not reset the machine or run it. Tell the site contact and refer the leak and fault to the owner's service provider. If the contact confirms the model and the business has a manual for it, you can clean the fascia with the approved product and a damp cloth, avoiding the control panel and any vents.

workedExamples.situation: A customer's coffee machine has a manufacturer manual that says the group heads must not be wetted, and the booking asks you to clean the whole machine.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you clean the machine within the rule?
workedExamples.reasoning: The manufacturer rule is more protective than the booking's general wording, so it governs. Clean the external panels with a damp cloth and an approved product. Keep water away from the group heads and the drip tray outlets, and record that the group heads were excluded by the manufacturer rule. Report the disagreement to the supervisor.

equipmentAndPpe: Photographic record on a device, with the data plate in shot
The manufacturer's manual or care guide for the model, on the device or in the equipment record
The approved product list for the job, as set in the business materials
Gloves and eye protection as set by the business for the job

commonErrors.error: Assuming a model is cleaned the same way as the last one you cleaned.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the data plate and the manufacturer's current care instructions for each appliance on each job.

commonErrors.error: Not recording existing damage, so the business is blamed for a leak or scorch mark that was already there.
commonErrors.prevention: Photograph and record every visible fault before the first cleaning step, and tell the site contact.

commonErrors.error: Running a machine to see whether it still works before cleaning it.
commonErrors.prevention: Do not operate the appliance to test it. Record its state and refer any fault. Operation is outside cleaning scope.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: A leak under a running or recently used machine can create an electrical, slip or scald hazard. Record it, keep people away and refer it before you go further.

Manufacturer warranty conditions may exclude some cleaning methods or cleaning by a third party. Under Australian Consumer Law, consumer guarantees apply alongside any warranty and a warranty cannot remove them.
This lesson does not grant a licence or authority to diagnose or repair an appliance fault.

qualityStandard: Make, model and serial number, or the reason they are missing, are recorded before any cleaning starts
The manufacturer's care instructions are read and the cleaning method for each part is recorded
Every visible fault and leak is recorded with a photograph before the first cleaning step
documentationEvidence: Make, model, serial number and location of each appliance
A photograph of the data plate and of each pre-existing fault
The name of the manual or care guide used, with its version or date where shown
summary: Confirm the make and model from the data plate before you clean.
The manufacturer's care instructions govern the method. Where they conflict with the business procedure, the more protective rule applies.
Record the pre-clean condition with photographs, and do not run or reset the machine.

knowledgeChecks.question: Where should you look first to find out the approved cleaning method for a commercial oven?
options: The method you used on the last oven of the same brand
The product label, since it lists dilution and contact time for the job
The manufacturer's care and cleaning instructions for that model
A forum post from another cleaner using the same product

knowledgeChecks.question: The data plate on an appliance is unreadable. What is the correct action?
options: Guess the model from its size and shape, then clean it as usual, since most commercial appliances use the same method
Ask the customer to run the machine so you can read the model number on the display while it is running, then record it
Skip the photograph because the appliance is obviously old, so there is little value in recording its condition
Record the visible brand and model, note the plate is unreadable, and use the most conservative method until the rules are confirmed

knowledgeChecks.question: Before cleaning, you notice a wet patch under a fryer and a fault code on the display. What should you do first?
options: Photograph and record the patch and the code, and refer the fault without resetting or running the fryer
Mop the patch and clean the fryer as booked, since a small wet area is not a fault that changes the job
Press the reset button to clear the code, then check whether the patch has dried before starting the clean
Ask the customer to switch on the fryer to see if the code goes away, then start the clean once it is stable

knowledgeChecks.question: The manufacturer says the group heads of a coffee machine must not be wetted, but the booking asks for the whole machine to be cleaned. Which rule governs?
options: The booking, because the customer is the one paying for the whole machine
The manufacturer rule, because it is the more protective instruction
Whichever rule is quicker to follow on the day, so the crew can finish
Neither, so the machine should not be cleaned at all until the rules agree

knowledgeChecks.question: Why is a pre-clean photograph of existing damage valuable?
options: It lets the worker skip the manufacturer's instructions for that model and clean straight away, which shortens the visit and the paperwork needed
It proves the worker holds a current licence for this appliance type, so the photograph can stand in as the licence record for the job file
It shows the customer how the machine looked before the job started, which protects the worker and the business from being blamed for pre-existing faults
It replaces the need to read the manufacturer's manual before cleaning, since the photo already shows the approved method for the model
